sections.title: Mental model — one door vs two doors

blocks.md: **Stack: one door (top). Queue: two doors (back enters, front exits). Everything else is discipline.**

steps: STACK push(A) push(B) push(C) → pop returns C, then B, then A
QUEUE enqueue(A) enqueue(B) enqueue(C) → dequeue returns A, then B, then C
Both O(1) per op when built right

st.append(20)

st.pop()               # POP

items.title: Implement Stack Class (vector-backed)

solutionCode.label: thin adapter over a vector, with guards on every read

items.complexity: push/pop/top/empty/size all O(1). push is amortised O(1) because the backing vector doubles.

followups.q: Why is push amortised O(1) rather than plain O(1)?
followups.a: When the vector fills, it allocates a bigger buffer and copies everything — an O(n) operation. But doubling means that happens only every n pushes, so the cost spread across all pushes is constant. Any single push can still be O(n); the average never is.

followups.q: Why does the top of the stack live at the END of the vector?
followups.a: Because push_back and pop_back are O(1), while inserting or erasing at the front is O(n) — every other element shifts. Mapping the stack top to the vector back is what makes the adapter free.

items.title: Implement Stack via Linked List
items.statement: Head = top; push/pop at head O(1).

solutionCode.label: head is the top; both operations are head operations

items.complexity: push/pop/top all O(1) worst case — no reallocation, unlike the vector version. Space O(n) with a pointer of overhead per element.

followups.q: Why the head and not the tail?
followups.a: A singly linked list can insert and delete at the head in O(1) with only a head pointer. Doing it at the tail needs the tail's predecessor, which costs an O(n) walk on every pop. The stack's LIFO discipline happens to match exactly what a singly linked list is good at.

followups.q: Which backing store would you pick in practice?
followups.a: The vector, almost always. It has no per-element pointer overhead and its elements are contiguous, so pushes and pops stay in cache. The linked version wins only when you need a hard worst-case O(1) push with no reallocation pause — real-time systems, not interviews.

items.title: Queue via Array (wasteful version OK)
items.statement: front/back indices; note the drifting-space problem aloud.
hints: front++ on dequeue wastes cells — that pain motivates circular queues later.

solutionCode.label: two indices, and the drifting-space problem stated out loud

items.complexity: enqueue and dequeue both O(1), but the array is consumed: after n dequeues the front index has walked to the end and the reclaimed cells are unusable.

followups.q: Demonstrate the leak concretely.
followups.a: With capacity 3: enqueue three, dequeue three. The queue is empty and holds nothing, but back == 3 == capacity, so the next enqueue fails. Three cells sit unused behind front. wastedCells() returns 3 — the waste is measurable, not hypothetical.

followups.q: What does the circular queue change?
followups.a: Indices wrap with modulo capacity, so dequeued cells are reused. That needs a separate count (or one sacrificed slot) to distinguish full from empty, since front == back is then ambiguous. Trading one extra field for full capacity reuse is the whole design.

items.title: Queue via Linked List
items.statement: Maintain BOTH head and tail pointers.
hints: Single-element dequeue must reset tail too.

solutionCode.label: head for dequeue, tail for enqueue, both maintained together

items.complexity: enqueue and dequeue both O(1) worst case. No capacity limit and no wasted cells.

followups.q: What breaks if dequeue forgets to reset tail?
followups.a: After removing the last element, head is null but tail still points at the freed node. The next enqueue takes the non-empty branch and writes tail->next on a dangling pointer — in C++ that is undefined behaviour, and in Python it silently resurrects a detached node that head never sees. It is the single most common bug in this class.

followups.q: Why does enqueue go at the tail and dequeue at the head?
followups.a: FIFO needs insertion at one end and removal at the other. Removal must be at the head because a singly linked list cannot cheaply remove its tail — that needs the predecessor. So the head is forced to be the exit, and the tail becomes the entrance.

items.title: Reverse String Using Stack
items.statement: Push all chars, pop builds reverse.

solutionCode.label: push everything, pop everything — LIFO reverses for free

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the stack.

followups.q: Why is a stack the natural tool for reversal?
followups.a: Last in, first out means the first character pushed is the last popped — the definition of reversal. You are not implementing reversal so much as reading the stack's own ordering. Any problem phrased as "process in reverse arrival order" is a stack problem.

followups.q: Is this the best way to reverse a string?
followups.a: No — two pointers swapping inward is O(1) space and touches each character once. The stack version costs O(n) extra memory to achieve the same thing. It earns its place only as a demonstration of LIFO, or when the input is a stream you cannot index.

items.title: Bracket Match — single type '(' ')'
items.statement: Balanced or not for one bracket type.

solutionCode.label: a counter suffices when there is only one bracket type

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) with the counter (a full stack is unnecessary for a single bracket type).

followups.q: Why are BOTH conditions needed?
followups.a: The negative check catches ")(" — balanced by count but invalidly ordered. The final-zero check catches "((" — never negative but left open. Either alone accepts a wrong string, so both are load-bearing.

followups.q: Why does one bracket type not need a stack?
followups.a: A stack stores WHICH bracket is open, but with a single type there is nothing to distinguish — only how many. The counter is the stack collapsed to its size. Add a second bracket type and the identity matters again, which is exactly K201.

items.title: Decimal to Binary via Stack
items.statement: Print binary of n using stack (remainders pop out MSB-first).
hints: Pop-all prints correct order — LIFO magic.

solutionCode.label: remainders come out LSB-first; the stack flips them
solutionCode.py:
def to_binary(n: int) -> str:
    if n == 0:
        return "0"                 # the loop emits nothing for 0
    neg = n < 0
    v = abs(n)
    st = []
    while v:
        st.append(v % 2)           # LSB pushed first
        v //= 2
    out = "".join(str(st.pop()) for _ in range(len(st)))   # MSB pops first
    return "-" + out if neg else out

items.complexity: Time O(log n) — one iteration per bit. Space O(log n) for the stack.

followups.q: Why does n = 0 need a special case?
followups.a: The while loop tests v as truthy, so it never runs for 0 and the stack stays empty — producing "". Zero is the one value whose correct output is not generated by the digit-extraction loop, exactly as in the recursive digit problems.

followups.q: What is the stack actually doing here?
followups.a: Reversing. Repeated division yields digits least-significant first, but written form is most-significant first. The stack is a reversal buffer — you could equally build the string and reverse it, or prepend each digit. The stack version makes the LIFO relationship explicit.

items.title: Undo/Redo Simulator
items.statement: Commands typed; UNDO moves top to redo-stack; REDO reverses it; new command clears redo.
hints: Clear redo on fresh input — classic editor semantics.

solutionCode.label: two stacks, and a fresh command clears redo

items.complexity: All operations O(1). Space O(number of commands).

followups.q: Why must a new command clear the redo stack?
followups.a: Redo replays a future that was undone. Once you type something new, that future never happened — replaying it would interleave commands that were never adjacent and corrupt the document. Every real editor does this, and forgetting it is the classic bug in a home-grown undo system.

followups.q: What would a tree-structured undo change?
followups.a: It keeps the abandoned branch instead of discarding it, so you can navigate back to the alternate future — Vim's undo tree and Emacs undo-tree work this way. The cost is a UI problem: users understand a linear stack, and a branching history needs a way to visualise it.

items.title: Next Greater Element — BRUTE force
items.statement: O(n²) version first — feel the pain the monotonic stack cures next level.
hints: For each i scan rightward until bigger found.

solutionCode.label: nested scan, deliberately naive

items.complexity: Time O(n^2) worst case — a decreasing array makes every inner scan run to the end. Space O(1) beyond the output. This is the pain the monotonic stack removes.

followups.q: Which input is the worst case, and why?
followups.a: A strictly decreasing array. No element ever finds a greater one to its right, so every inner loop runs to the end without breaking — n(n-1)/2 comparisons and every answer is -1. An increasing array is the best case: each inner loop breaks immediately, giving O(n).

followups.q: What does the monotonic stack exploit that this ignores?
followups.a: This version re-scans the same elements for every i, throwing away everything it learned. The stack keeps a decreasing sequence of unresolved indices, so each element is pushed and popped at most once — O(n) total. The insight is that once an element is passed by something bigger, it can never be an answer again.

items.title: Queue Reversal
items.statement: Reverse a queue using a stack.

solutionCode.label: drain the queue into a stack, then drain the stack back

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the stack.

followups.q: Why does passing through a stack reverse a queue?
followups.a: The queue emits front-first; the stack returns last-pushed-first. Composing a FIFO read with a LIFO read inverts the order exactly once. Passing through a second stack would restore the original order — the reversal is the ordering mismatch, not the container.

followups.q: Could recursion replace the explicit stack?
followups.a: Yes — dequeue one element, recurse on the rest, then enqueue that element on the unwind. The call stack IS the stack. It is elegant but costs O(n) frames and dies on large queues, which is the same trade discussed in the recursion module.
